chunks.text: Around 1250, power in western Europe was decentralized rather than concentrated in a capital. A peasant's real ruler was the local lord of the manor, while kings had limited power and depended on lords to supply soldiers, so authority was scattered down a ladder of personal loyalties.

Compared with Song China's centralized bureaucracy and the sophisticated common culture of Dar al-Islam, western Europe around 1200 was comparatively poor, rural, decentralized, and something of a backwater. This makes the later 'rise of the West' a genuine historical puzzle to explain.

Feudalism was the political-military system of medieval Europe in which a lord granted land, called a fief, to a vassal, who in return owed military service, loyalty, and counsel. Kings granted land to great nobles, who granted portions to lesser knights, producing a chain of personal obligations rather than a centralized state.

Manorialism was the economic system underlying feudalism. A manor was a largely self-sufficient agricultural estate where the lord's land was worked by peasants, producing most of what it needed and trading little, so it was an economy of land and obligation rather than money and markets.

Serfs were peasants who were legally bound to the manor's land, unable to leave without permission and owing labor and a share of their crops to the lord in exchange for protection and the right to farm. They were not enslaved but were not free to move.

Europe was decentralized largely because no strong central state arose after the fall of the western Roman Empire. In a dangerous, fragmented world, people traded freedom for protection, with serfs bound to defending lords and knights bound to greater lords who organized defense.

The Roman Catholic Church was the closest thing to a unifying authority in fragmented western Europe. Nearly everyone was Catholic, the Pope in Rome claimed spiritual authority over all of them, and church law shaped marriage, morality, and the calendar of festivals.

The Catholic Church was enormously wealthy and powerful in worldly terms, one of the largest landholders in Europe, collecting tithes and able to influence kings. Monasteries also preserved literacy and copied ancient texts, keeping classical learning alive through centuries when few could read.

The Schism of 1054 divided Christianity into the Roman Catholic Church in the west, led by the Pope, and the Eastern Orthodox Church in the east, centered on the Byzantine Empire and Constantinople. Christianity was therefore not a single unified faith in this period.

The Byzantine Empire was the surviving eastern half of the Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, and was far more centralized, urban, and wealthy than western Europe. It spread Eastern Orthodox Christianity, its alphabet, and its culture north into the Slavic world, including Russia.

In a politically decentralized Europe, the Catholic Church provided a shared identity, a common scholarly language (Latin), and a shared moral framework. It played a unifying cultural role similar to Confucianism in East Asia or Islam in Dar al-Islam.

The Crusades were a series of religious wars beginning in 1095 that aimed to seize the Holy Land from Muslim control. They failed in their main military goal but reconnected western Europeans with the richer Islamic Mediterranean and Byzantium, bringing back goods and knowledge and helping revive long-distance trade.

Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa grew wealthy acting as middlemen in the revived Mediterranean trade after the Crusades. Their commerce helped fuel the growth of towns and a money economy in Europe.

As commerce expanded in late medieval Europe, towns swelled with merchants and artisans who stood outside the feudal-manorial order, and a new urban middle class emerged. Money increasingly mattered more than land and obligation, gradually undermining the old system.

In 1215, English nobles forced King John to sign the Magna Carta, which limited royal power. It planted an early seed of the idea that even a king is bound by law, even as monarchs in England and France worked to centralize power.

During the late medieval period, some European kings began to centralize power at the expense of the nobility, building the foundations of strong monarchies in places such as England and France. This slowly reversed the extreme decentralization of feudalism.

The Black Death was a devastating plague that swept Europe between roughly 1347 and 1351, killing perhaps a third of the population. It traveled along Afro-Eurasian trade networks, showing that connection spread disease as well as goods.

Because the Black Death killed so many workers, surviving peasants in much of western Europe could demand wages and freedom, fatally weakening serfdom and the manorial system. Labor became precious and the old feudal bonds loosened.

Out of late medieval Europe's revived trade and social upheaval, the Renaissance, a flowering of art and learning drawing on rediscovered classical knowledge, was just beginning in the wealthy cities of Italy by around 1450.

Comparison is a historical reasoning skill central to AP World History. A strong comparison identifies a genuine similarity and a meaningful difference between societies and, crucially, explains WHY those similarities or differences existed, rather than merely describing each society.

Song China and feudal Europe were both large agrarian societies facing the challenge of organizing power over many people, but they answered it oppositely: China centralized through a bureaucracy of exam-chosen scholar-officials funded by a commercial economy, while Europe decentralized power among hereditary feudal lords with the Catholic Church providing cultural unity.

The difference between centralized China and decentralized Europe flowed from circumstance: China had a long unbroken tradition of imperial unity and the wealth to fund a salaried bureaucracy, while western Europe had fragmented after the western Roman Empire collapsed and lacked a strong central state.

A comparison long essay (LEQ) is scored on contextualization (setting the stage), a defensible comparative thesis, specific evidence for BOTH societies, and historical reasoning that analyzes why similarities or differences existed. Describing only one society or comparing across mismatched time periods loses points.

Common comparison-essay mistakes include the 'parallel description' trap of describing two societies without connecting them, neglecting one of the two societies, and using evidence from outside the prompt's time period. Graders ignore out-of-period evidence and require both societies to be analyzed.

Useful categories for comparing states from c. 1200 to c. 1450 include political structure (centralized versus decentralized), economy, religion and sources of legitimacy, labor systems, and attitudes toward trade. These categories work for any regions, such as China and Europe, the Aztec and Inca, or Mali and the Swahili coast.

Europe's fragmentation into competing kingdoms and rival merchant cities bred relentless competition that would later drive innovation, exploration, and the race for trade routes, since no single emperor could halt a new idea or risky voyage. This competitive dynamic is part of the explanation for the later rise of European global power.
